opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly, it's one I've gone back and forth on over the years.

I think force and tactile information are fundamentally important for manipulation, more than most of us in robot learning have acknowledged in practice. If you watch how humans manipulate objects, so much of it is driven by contact. Inserting a plug, wiping a table, turning a key, picking up something fragile: vision tells you roughly where things are and what you want to do, but the actual execution, the moment-to-moment adjustment, is governed by what you feel. There are classic studies where people's fingertips are anesthetized, and their dexterity collapses even though their vision is completely intact.

So why has the field been so vision-centric? Part of it is practical. Cameras are cheap, standardized, and robust, and we have huge amounts of pretrained visual representations from internet data. Tactile sensors, by contrast, have historically been fragile, expensive, hard to calibrate, and every sensor produces a different kind of signal. There's no "ImageNet for touch." So if you're trying to scale up data collection and learning, vision is the path of least resistance.

There's also a data-collection problem that's subtle. A lot of our demonstration data comes from teleoperation, and in most teleoperation setups the human operator doesn't actually feel what the robot feels. So the demonstrations themselves don't really encode force-aware behavior. The human is compensating visually, slowly and carefully, and the policy learns that visual strategy. If you want policies that truly exploit touch, you need the demonstrator to be in the haptic loop, through force feedback, or through approaches where humans do the task with their own hands while we capture the contact information.

How I think about the role going forward is roughly as a hierarchy. Vision and language are great for the high-level "what" and "where": task understanding, scene understanding, long-horizon planning. Force and touch are essential for the low-level "how," the contact-rich, closed-loop control where precision and reactivity matter. Within that, I'd distinguish two uses. One is reactive: detecting slip, regulating grip force, complying when you hit something unexpected. The other is perceptual: using touch to infer properties you can't see, like friction, mass, stiffness, or the pose of an object occluded by your own hand.

I'm optimistic because the hardware is getting better and cheaper, and people are starting to build multimodal policies that fuse vision and touch in a principled way. But I think the real unlock is going to be data, figuring out how to collect large, diverse datasets where contact information is a first-class citizen rather than an afterthought. Once we have that, I suspect we'll see a big jump in the kinds of dexterous, contact-rich tasks robots can do reliably.

r001.rationale: The response discusses tactile sensing as information for perception and force as part of control, but it does not raise whether force or tactile information should be used on the input side or output side of learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, partly because so much of the recent progress in robot learning has been driven by vision. We've gotten really good at taking images, running them through big pretrained models, and getting policies that do interesting things. And I think that's great, but it also creates a bit of a blind spot, because vision is fundamentally a remote sensing modality. It tells you about the world at a distance. The moment your robot actually makes contact with something, a lot of what matters is no longer visible.

Think about something like inserting a plug, or threading a cable, or wiping a table. The camera might be occluded by the gripper, or the relevant signal is a few millimeters of misalignment that you just can't resolve from pixels. But you can feel it. You feel the resistance, you feel the slip, you feel when the part seats correctly. Humans rely on this constantly, and we barely notice because it's so automatic.

So I think force and tactile sensing are essential for the "last inch" of manipulation, the part that happens during contact. The challenge is that it's much harder to learn from than vision. There's less data, the sensors are heterogeneous across robots, the signals are high-frequency and noisy, and we don't have the equivalent of internet-scale pretraining for touch. You can't scrape a billion tactile images.

The way I think about it is that force and tactile information should be the thing that lets the policy be reactive, rather than just planning from a snapshot. Vision gives you the coarse plan: where the object is, roughly how to approach. Force and touch close the loop at a much finer timescale. And a lot of the interesting research questions are about how to combine those: how do you represent tactile signals in a way that transfers across sensors, how do you teach a policy to use force feedback without needing tons of demonstrations, and how do you collect that data in the first place, since a lot of teleoperation setups don't give the human a good sense of touch either.

My honest view is that we've been able to get surprisingly far with vision alone, and that's maybe made the field a little complacent. But if we want robots doing real, dexterous, contact-rich tasks reliably, I don't think we get there without taking touch seriously.

r001.rationale: The response describes force and touch as feedback used by the policy, but does not raise whether they belong on the input side or the output side of learning.

astra-6.text:
I think force and tactile information are really important, especially when we’re talking about learning to manipulate objects. Vision gives you a lot of information about where things are and how to approach them. But once you make contact, you need to understand what’s happening at that interface. Is the object slipping? Are you pushing too hard? Is something getting stuck? Those things can be difficult to infer from vision alone.

The interesting question for learning is how to bring these signals together. You don’t necessarily want a separate visual policy and a separate tactile policy. You want the robot to use whatever information is useful at that moment—to use vision to reach toward an object, and then use touch and force to adjust its grasp or respond to resistance.

There’s also a practical challenge: collecting useful tactile data consistently across different sensors and robot platforms. So I see it as both a sensing problem and a learning problem. Having the sensor is one piece; learning how to use that feedback to make better decisions is the other.

r001.rationale: The response discusses combining vision, touch, and force as feedback for decisions, but it does not raise whether force or tactile information belongs on the input side or the output side of learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think force and tactile information are really important because they tell you things that are hard to infer from vision alone. You can see where an object is, but once you make contact, you need to know: Am I actually holding it? Is it slipping? Am I pushing too hard? Those are central questions for manipulation.

From a learning perspective, the interesting question is how to combine those signals. Vision gives you a broader picture of the scene, while touch gives you very local information about the interaction. And your actions affect what you can observe—you might press or move something a little bit to understand it better.

So I see touch as both a signal for controlling the robot and a way to learn about the world. The challenge is getting enough useful interaction data and learning representations that generalize across objects and tasks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses combining vision and touch and describes touch as useful for control and learning, but it does not raise whether force or tactile information belongs on the input side or output side of learning.
